outcomes.reply: Right. Once the vein is closed, the tumor’s adrenaline has no route into the blood. The anesthetist needs warning, because the pressure can fall quickly when it comes out.

outcomes.story: You suggest a biopsy. The surgeon says never.
outcomes.reply: A needle into this tumor can release a flood of adrenaline or make it bleed. The blood tests and the scan already tell us what it is.

outcomes.story: You say the anesthetist does not need to know. The anesthetist looks over the drape.
outcomes.reply: They very much do. His pressure can spike while the tumor is handled and drop the moment it is out. They have to be ready for both.

5.resident: The tumor is out and he is recovering well. Remember his uncle’s thyroid cancer and his aunt’s adrenal tumors.
5.question: What should happen next?
options: Reassure him, with no more tests
Refer him for genetic counseling and testing, and check for the tumors that travel with this one
Start lifelong high-dose steroids
Remove his other adrenal gland now

terms.meaning: Passed down in a family through a gene.
An inherited condition that causes adrenal tumors, a type of thyroid cancer and overactive parathyroid glands.

outcomes.story: You say he needs nothing more. The resident disagrees.
outcomes.reply: Up to four in ten of these tumors run in families. With his family history, stopping here could miss a thyroid cancer in him or in his relatives.

outcomes.story: You book the genetics referral. The counselor will also offer testing to his relatives if a gene is found.
outcomes.reply: Good. If he carries one of these genes, we screen his thyroid and his other adrenal gland, and his family can be tested too.

outcomes.story: You suggest lifelong steroids. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: His other adrenal gland is healthy and makes all the cortisol he needs. He does not need replacement.

outcomes.story: You suggest removing the other gland. The surgeon says no.
outcomes.reply: There is no tumor in it. Taking it out would leave him dependent on steroid tablets for life, for nothing.

differential.resident: The hormone tests and the scan are in his chart.
differential.question: What is the lump?
options: A tumor making too much cortisol (Cushing syndrome)
A tumor making too much aldosterone (Conn syndrome)
A tumor making adrenaline-type hormones (pheochromocytoma)
A harmless fatty lump in the adrenal gland
differential.reveal: It is a pheochromocytoma, a tumor of the adrenal gland that releases adrenaline and noradrenaline in bursts. That explains the attacks and the stubborn blood pressure. His cortisol and aldosterone tests are normal, and a harmless lump would look fatty on the scan and clear the dye quickly.

terms.meaning: A tumor of the adrenal gland’s inner part that makes adrenaline-type hormones.
A sudden attack of symptoms that comes and goes.

ending.stable: Home after surgery with a normal blood pressure, and a genetics appointment booked
ending.worse: Home after surgery, after a blood pressure crisis in clinic that could have been avoided
ending.critical: In intensive care after a blood pressure crisis

gs-052.plainDiagnosis: An adrenal gland tumor that releases bursts of adrenaline (pheochromocytoma).

science.title: Why the tumor would not switch off
science.text: A healthy adrenal gland releases adrenaline only when nerves tell it to, and stops when the signal stops. The tumor ignores those signals and releases it whenever it is squeezed or stirred, which is why bending over could set off an attack.

science.title: Why adrenaline drives blood pressure up
science.text: Blood pressure depends on how hard the heart pumps and on how narrow the vessels are. Adrenaline-type hormones do both: they narrow the vessels through alpha receptors and drive the heart through beta receptors. Blocking alpha opens the vessels again.

sources.title: Lenders et al. (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2014): pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline
Neumann, Young and Eng (N Engl J Med 2019): pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma
